brief.notification_title: Tech leads, oil eases; Fed and Big Tech up next
brief.market_summary: At midday in New York, stocks are higher and AI names are leading. The S&P 500 is up 0.70% at 7,730.61, the Nasdaq is up 1.27% and SMH is up 2.88%. The lift comes from the Anthropic IPO filing and Broadcom arranging chip financing for Anthropic, plus US data that came in well above forecasts. Treasuries barely moved: the 10Y is at 4.986%, flat on the day but 25bp lower over a month, as markets wait for Wednesday's FOMC. The Fed is expected to hold, but a December hike is largely priced. Brent's snapshot shows -5.5% to $109.43, but that compares two different futures contracts. The real move was about -1% (BNO -0.97%, December Brent near $114.9), on talks with Iran over Hormuz. Bitcoin is flat at $80.5K while ETH and the smaller L1s keep sliding.
brief.since_last:
1) US data came in hot. Conference Board confidence was 91.7 vs 81.0 expected, durable goods +1.8% vs +0.6%, the Dallas Fed index 13.4 vs 8.8 and the Chicago Fed index 0.07 vs -0.10. The underlying business-investment numbers were softer, though: core capital goods +0.5% vs +0.7%.
2) The AI trade revived. The Anthropic IPO filing, Broadcom's financing for Anthropic, and Nvidia and AMD investing $4bn in Meta as Meta raises $95bn (n104, n48) sent SMH up 2.9%.
3) Earnings were mostly beats. UPS beat and raised guidance; Coca-Cola beat and raised but North American volume was weak; PayPal beat on EPS and missed on revenue; SoFi is up 15%. Boeing missed (adjusted -$0.34 vs -$0.21) and is down 9% because the 737 ramp slips to late 2027.
4) Oil: an Oman-brokered outline to restore free navigation through Hormuz and Iranian talk of terms to end the war (n3) are pushing prices down. Attacks near Ras Tanura (n113) and by the Houthis are holding them up. OPEC+ is expected to keep quotas unchanged on Sunday (n43).
5) Crypto: spot BTC ETFs took in +$110.3m on 26 Oct, ending a two-day outflow streak. ETH ETFs lost -$88.6m, though that day's data may be incomplete.

economic_data.takeaway: This was the first rise in four months (n38) and a very large beat; lower gas prices helped (n57). Strong consumers make it easier for Warsh to keep a hiking bias, which supports the 84% December-hike pricing. It is good for cyclicals but not for rate cuts.
Non-defence aircraft orders (+28.4%) drove most of the headline. Read the core figures below rather than the headline.
This is a slight miss. Ex-transport orders were +0.5% vs +0.6%. Business investment outside AI is firm but not booming, so the data is less hot than the headline suggests.
Activity is back at about trend growth. Together with GDPNow at 3.5%, it argues against any talk of cuts.
Texas factories are accelerating, helped by $100+ oil. It adds to the evidence that growth is not slowing.
Demand was soft: bid-to-cover 2.59 vs a 2.64 average, and indirect bidders took 45.7% vs a 58.3% average (graded C-). Buyers are cautious about front-end duration before the Fed.
Bills still yield above 4%, which pays you to wait out the event cluster.

A hold is near-certain (93-94% of surveyed economists). What matters is whether Warsh endorses the roughly 84% priced December hike. If he does, the dollar firms, the front end sells off and long-duration tech is pressured. If he leans dovish, duration and BTC rally.
A print at or above 3.5% on top of today's data would cement a December hike and test the 10Y's recent rally.
This is the key inflation print. A 0.4% would push the 10Y back toward 5.15%, my trigger to start adding duration. A 0.2% would support bonds.
If wage growth cools, it partly offsets hawkish inflation worries.

earnings.result: Adjusted EPS -$0.34 vs -$0.21 expected (a miss). Revenue $24.19bn vs $23.84bn. Free cash flow $0.5bn; record $745bn backlog. No significant 737 MAX ramp until late 2027; 2026 delivery target of 500 likely missed.
earnings.takeaway: The stock is down about 9%. Investors were paying for the production ramp, and it has slipped a year. The price-weighted Dow (+0.16%) is lagging the S&P because of it. The XLI read-through is limited (XLI +0.41%).

earnings.result: Adjusted EPS $1.69 vs $1.63. Revenue ~$22.9bn vs $22.29bn. Full-year guidance raised for the second straight quarter: ~$92.6bn revenue, ~$7.28 EPS.
earnings.takeaway: The stock is up about 2%. Freight volumes are holding up, consistent with today's strong activity data.

earnings.result: Adjusted EPS $0.91 vs $0.87-0.88 expected. Revenue $13.4bn (+7%) vs $12.9bn. Comparable EPS growth guidance raised to at least 11%. North American volume was weak.
earnings.takeaway: Shares slipped despite beating and raising, after a 32% gain this year. Staples (XLP -0.68%) are being sold as money rotates back into tech.

earnings.result: Adjusted EPS $1.45 vs $1.31. Revenue $8.58bn vs $8.71bn (a miss). Full-year EPS guidance raised to ~$5.60, with job cuts.
earnings.takeaway: This is a cost-cutting story, not a growth story. The stock swung from about -2% pre-market to about +2% intraday.

earnings.result: Adjusted EPS $0.18 vs $0.17. Revenue $1.37bn vs $1.28bn. Guidance raised.
earnings.takeaway: Up about 15%, so retail-fintech risk appetite is alive. Robinhood reports tonight against that bar.

earnings.result: EPS $3.16 vs $2.89 (+9.3% surprise). Outlook raised on AI data-centre demand.
earnings.takeaway: Up about 9.7% after hours, confirming AI hardware demand before the Microsoft and Alphabet capex updates on Wednesday.
A small miss, but the stock rose about 2.6% after hours, so investors focused on chip-design demand rather than the penny miss.

earnings.result: Hartford $3.50 vs $3.15 (+11%). Cincinnati Financial $2.86 vs $1.99 (+44%). Principal Financial missed ($2.22 vs $2.46).
earnings.takeaway: Property and casualty insurers' underwriting is strong this quarter. XLF is flat (-0.14%), so it isn't moving the sector.

earnings.result: Estimated EPS: Visa $3.43 (vs $2.98 a year ago), Robinhood $0.56, Seagate $7.17 (vs $2.51).
earnings.takeaway: Visa is a check on consumer spending after the confidence beat. Robinhood reads across to crypto trading and tokenized stocks (n100). Seagate tests AI storage demand before Sandisk on Thursday.

earnings.result: Estimated EPS: Microsoft $4.71 (vs $4.13), Alphabet $2.94 (vs $2.87). Microsoft will disclose Azure revenue (n33).
earnings.takeaway: They report about two hours after Warsh speaks. Capex guidance drives the semis rally (SMH is -7% over a month). Weak cloud growth or a capex pullback would undo today's AI bounce.
This is the gate for adding the second half of XLE. Watch buyback and capex plans at $100+ oil and whether management assumes the war premium lasts.

sections.summary: Broad gains led by AI. The Nasdaq is up 1.27% and semis 2.88% on the Anthropic IPO, Broadcom's chip financing for Anthropic and Nvidia and AMD's stakes in Meta. Defensives are lagging and energy is down 1.8% as oil eases. The VIX is 17.54. Mega-cap earnings and the Fed land within 24 hours of each other on Wednesday, so this rally has not yet been tested.
key_points: Leaders: SMH +2.88%, XLK +1.89%, Broadcom +4.1%. Laggards: XLE -1.79%, XLP -0.68%. SMH is still -7.1% over a month.
Earnings were mostly beat-and-raise (UPS, Coca-Cola, PayPal EPS, SoFi, Celestica). Boeing is the big miss.
Risks: a 50% tariff threat on Canadian autos (n6), and AI-bubble worries (n18, n4) ahead of Microsoft and Alphabet on Wednesday.

sections.summary: Treasuries ignored a round of strong data. The 10Y is flat at 4.986% after a 25bp rally over the past month. The front end is cautious: the 2Y auction tailed slightly and foreign demand was weak, with a December hike about 84% priced. Credit is firm, with HYG up 0.38% and LQD up 0.29%.
key_points: Official curve (26 Oct): 2s10s +32bp, 3m10y +78bp. The 6M bill rose 5bp, a sign hikes are being priced.
2Y auction 4.708%, 0.3bp tail; indirects 45.7% vs 58.3% average. Bills: 3M 4.050%, 6M 4.210%.
Other central banks are tightening too: the BoC is about 80% priced to hike, the RBNZ to hike, and UK CPI is 3.5%. JPMorgan's Michele sees 7-8% bond returns over 12 months (n149).

sections.summary: The snapshot's -5.51% to $109.43 compares the January contract with Monday's December close (above $116). That gap is curve structure, not a crash. December Brent was about $114.9 (-0.8%) and BNO is -0.97%. Diplomacy, including an Omani outline to reopen Hormuz and Iranian talk of end-of-war terms, is pushing against continued attacks on Saudi infrastructure.
key_points: BZ=F (January) $109.43. December was about $114.9 on Tuesday morning. That is roughly $5 of backwardation between consecutive months, a sign of acute shortage.
WTI $100.06 (-1.67%). BNO $69.39 (-0.97% on the day, +15.0% over a month vs +3.9% for the continuous Brent series).
Supporting prices: a fire near Ras Tanura after an attack (n113), Houthi strikes, the US SPR at its lowest since 1982, and UBS seeing Brent near $110 by year-end (n95).
Pushing prices down: Iran talks (n3), an estimated ~$20 geopolitical premium, and OPEC+ expected to keep quotas unchanged Sunday (n43). API and EIA inventory reports are due Tuesday and Wednesday.

sections.summary: Bitcoin is holding near $80.5K, supported by renewed ETF inflows, but it is not participating in the equity rally. ETH and the smaller L1s keep losing ground, with ETF outflows from ETH and SOL. Hawkish-Fed risk, a firmer dollar and net-short whale positioning argue against buying the dip before Wednesday.
key_points: BTC $80,506 (+0.2%, -5.6% over a month). ETH $2,345.66 (-14.0% over a month). SOL $100.87 (-18.4%). SUI -26.8% and TON -24.2% over a month.
Spot ETF flows on 26 Oct: BTC +$110.3m after a $774m outflow streak; ETH -$88.6m; SOL -$8.2m. Prior week: BTC +$442.7m, ETH -$225.0m.
Hyperliquid whales have turned net short (n12). Ark sold $15m of its own BTC ETF (n73). Big BTC options expiry ahead (~$10.8bn, n111).
XRP +1.7% on Ripple's RLUSD deal with Robinhood (n50). Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood report this week.

brief.instructor_take: My read is that today's rally is real, but the market is pricing it as if Wednesday were a non-event, and I don't think it is. Look at the sequence. Warsh speaks at 14:30 ET Wednesday, Microsoft and Alphabet report about two hours later, and core PCE and GDP land at 08:30 Thursday. That is three binary events in about 18 hours, all landing on the same crowded AI-and-duration trade. The crowd is anchored on "93% hold." The tradeable question is whether Warsh confirms a December hike, and today's data makes that easier for him: confidence beat by 10 points and the Dallas Fed, Chicago Fed and durable-goods headline all beat. What a less experienced investor misses is that the 10Y has rallied 25bp in a month, mostly on hopes that oil will fall, while hike odds rose. That gap closes either through peace in the Gulf or through a hot PCE, and I can't tell you which comes first. So I'm not adding equity or crypto risk today. I'm keeping cash in bills at about 4%, holding the energy position I already have, and staying out of the crypto assets with the weakest ETF flows. Read that -5.5% Brent figure with care: it is mostly the gap between two contract months, and BNO's -1% is the honest move. If we get through Thursday with the 10Y above 5.15% or the S&P down 3-5%, that is when I'd want to put money to work, not chase a 2.9% semis pop the day before the hardest test of the week.

top_ideas.title: Park dry powder in T-bills through Fed, PCE
top_ideas.one_liner: Bills pay ~4%+ to wait out Warsh, Big Tech and PCE
top_ideas.thesis: With an FOMC press conference, Microsoft and Alphabet earnings and core PCE all within 18 hours, the best reward for the risk sits in the shortest bills. SGOV earns about 4.05-4.2% with almost no price risk, and if a December hike arrives, its yield resets higher within weeks. It also keeps cash ready for a post-event pullback.
top_ideas.reasoning: Start with the evidence. Today's beats (confidence 91.7 vs 81.0, Dallas Fed 13.4 vs 8.8) strengthen the case for the roughly 84% priced December hike. The 6M bill rose 5bp on the official curve while the 10Y sat flat. The concept is duration risk versus reinvestment: a bill fund rolls into higher yields if the Fed hikes, while longer bonds lose price. I prefer SGOV to IEF because the 10Y has already rallied 25bp in a month, so there is less cushion if PCE comes in hot. The weak 2Y auction (indirects 45.7% vs 58.3%) also tells me buyers aren't eager for duration before the Fed. I prefer it to stocks this week because the S&P is roughly flat over the month, so you aren't missing a trend, and the risk is concentrated in two days. Two things would change my mind: Warsh opening the door to cuts, or the 10Y closing above 5.15% after PCE, which would make longer bonds cheap enough to start buying. The risk is opportunity cost if everything goes smoothly and stocks run, and I'm willing to pay that.

risks: Opportunity cost if the S&P extends its rally after the Fed and earnings

top_ideas.entry: Buy now with the earmarked cash; timing doesn't matter for a bill fund. Hold through Friday.
top_ideas.invalidation: Warsh signals near-term cuts: rotate a third into IEF. The 10Y closes above 5.15% after PCE: begin scaling a third into IEF. The S&P falls 3-5% with the VIX above 22: deploy part into equities.
top_ideas.sizing: The cash earmarked for new risk this month, typically 10-20% of the portfolio.

top_ideas.title: Hold half of XLE; add the rest after XOM/CVX
top_ideas.one_liner: Keep XLE half; add second half only after XOM/CVX Friday
top_ideas.thesis: Producers' earnings are roughly doubling year on year at $100+ crude, and the oil futures curve still shows acute shortage. Diplomacy over Hormuz is now the main risk, so hold the first half bought near $69 and make the second half conditional on Friday's reports and Brent holding $105.
top_ideas.reasoning: The fundamentals are strong. Consensus EPS is $3.90 for Exxon vs $1.88 a year ago and $4.78 for Chevron vs $1.85. The US SPR is at its lowest since 1982, and attacks near Ras Tanura show supply is still being hit. I own this through producers rather than BNO because the stocks don't price in the full war premium. If peace breaks out, XLE should fall less than crude, and it pays a dividend while you wait. What has changed since Monday is the diplomacy: Oman has an outline to restore navigation through Hormuz and Iran's leadership is discussing terms (n3). One analyst puts the premium at about $20, so a deal could hit crude hard and quickly. That is why I'm not adding before Friday. Don't be fooled by the -5.5% Brent figure; that is the December-to-January contract gap, and BNO's -1% is the real move. If XLE closes below $65.50 or front-month Brent settles below $100, the market is telling me the premium is unwinding and I'd exit. A signed Hormuz navigation agreement would also make me exit.

top_ideas.title: Stay out of ETH and alt L1s until flows turn
top_ideas.one_liner: ETH ETF outflows persist; no buying until $2,700 with inflows
top_ideas.thesis: Money is flowing into spot BTC ETFs and out of ETH and SOL ETFs, and the smaller L1s are down 18-27% over a month. With hawkish-Fed risk and whales positioned net short, there is no catalyst to own the weakest part of crypto this week.
top_ideas.reasoning: Relative strength is the concept: when the marginal buyer (ETF flows) favours one asset over its peers, the laggards keep lagging. Spot BTC ETFs took in $442.7m last week and $110.3m on Monday. ETH ETFs lost $225.0m and then $88.6m, and Solana funds saw outflows in nine of ten October sessions. Prices confirm it: ETH is -14.0% and SOL -18.4% over the month against BTC's -5.6%. Crypto didn't join today's equity rally, and a hawkish Warsh plus a firmer dollar (DXY 102.25) are headwinds for assets with no yield. I'll be candid that the 26 Oct ETH flow data may be incomplete; one source showed a $16.1m Fidelity inflow. One day doesn't change the trend. If you want crypto exposure, BTC through IBIT is the stronger asset, but I'd wait until after Wednesday. I'd change my mind if ETH reclaims $2,700 with three or more straight days of net ETF inflows.

brief.prior_ideas_review:
SGOV (buy): working as intended. It is earning carry with no drawdown, and the 3M bill auctioned at 4.050%. Neither trigger has fired: the Fed has not hinted at cuts and the 10Y is 4.986%, not above 5.15%. Keep.

XLE (add): the first half bought near $69 is at $68.39, about -1%. Neither invalidation has been hit: XLE is above $65.50 and January Brent is $109.43, above $100. De-escalation risk is rising, so keep the position but make the second half conditional on Friday's reports and Brent holding $105.

ETH (avoid): working. ETH is $2,345.66, -3.2% on the week, and never bounced to $2,500 to offer a trim. ETF outflows continued. Keep.

lesson.explanation: When a supply shock hits, buyers pay more for oil delivered now than for oil delivered later, so each later futures month trades cheaper. That shape is called backwardation. A 'continuous' futures price drops mechanically each time the quoted contract switches to the next, cheaper month, even if nothing happened in the market. A fund like BNO that sells the expiring contract and buys the next one buys it cheaper, and if prices hold, it earns that difference over time, which is called roll yield.
lesson.todays_example: The snapshot shows Brent -5.51% to $109.43. That compares the January contract with Monday's December close (above $116); December itself traded at about $114.9, -0.8%. The real move was about -1% (BNO -0.97%). Over the past month, BNO is +15.0% while the continuous Brent series is only +3.9%. The gap is roll yield from a market in steep backwardation.
